title: Timing the VIX futures premium
ask: Does the VIX futures basis still predict returns?
reason: No. The slope turned positive after 2014.
hypothesis: A steep VIX futures curve (front above spot) forecasts weak VX futures returns after the 2014 publication.
question: Two published rules short VIX futures when they trade far above spot VIX and buy them when they trade below it. Did the signal behind those rules keep working in the twelve years after the papers' samples ended?
prior: The papers are clean and the parameters are published, so there was little to tune. Against that: an out-of-sample replication of one rule came out slightly negative, and short-volatility products lost about 90% in February 2018. We put the chance of passing the gate at about one in three before starting.
citations: Cheng, I.-H. (2019). The VIX Premium. Review of Financial Studies 32(1), 180–227.
Simon, D. P. & Campasano, J. (2014). The VIX Futures Basis: Evidence and Trading Strategies. Journal of Derivatives 21(3), 54–69.
method: Built our own VX term structure from Cboe's free daily settlements of every monthly contract since March 2004, and checked it: no missing sessions, the 2007 price-scale change found from the data, and a 30-day constant-maturity index that tracks VIXY at a daily correlation of 0.996 since Cboe moved the settlement time to 16:00 ET in October 2020.

Kill test fixed in advance, before any trading rule was run: regress the next 21 sessions' log return of the rolled front future on the basis (front settle − spot VIX), daily from August 2014 (after Cheng's sample ends), with Newey-West errors at 20 lags. A slope at or above zero kills the sleeve.

Three trading variants were written down in advance (Cheng's short-or-flat rule, Simon–Campasano's 5-day long/short rule, and the better of the two hedged against SPY) with costs, fees, a full day's signal lag and stress-day sizing. None was run, because the kill test came first.
verdict_reason: Killed at the kill test. From August 2014 the slope is +0.0098 (Newey-West t +1.28, 3,050 days): a steeper curve did not forecast weaker futures returns, and if anything pointed slightly the other way. In the papers' own period (2004 to July 2014) the same regression gives −0.024 (t −2.41), so the signal was real and has since faded. What is still there is the plain volatility premium: VX futures lose money on average whatever the curve looks like (intercept −7.8% per 21 sessions, t −4.5). Collecting that unconditionally is a different strategy, which we did not pre-register, and it carries the February 2018 kind of loss.
lessons: A published predictor can be real in its sample and gone afterwards. Testing only on the years after publication is what showed it.
The cheap kill test settled it before any backtest of a trading rule, so there were no tuned variants to explain away.
The term-structure data was still useful: the same build fed the VIX curve de-risk trigger test, which was also archived (it switched on and off too fast and tripled the overlay's trading).
